a: Nope, there's no full version in the way you mean. Those scenes were shot specifically for the VH-1 special. Not everything has a secret director's cut.

subject: Why is my CD booKleT misprinted?
q: My Hounds of Love CD booklet says it includes the 12 inch version of Ruth, but the disc doesn't have it. Did someone switch my disc or is the booklet misprinted?
a: The booklet's misprinted. The CDs in several countries claim the 12 inch version, but as far as I know none actually have it. Nobody switched your disc, so relax.

subject: one question many thanks
q: What's the difference, other than the obvious, between the Japanese Kate Bush box set and the English one?
a: Covers differ for The Kick Inside and Never For Ever. The Japanese set has two booklets, a biography all in Japanese, and longer album booklets with lyrics in Japanese and English, including the two extra albums. That's the big one. Supposedly it sounds better, unconfirmed.

subject: "Jig of Life" question
q: Where does the spoken text in Kate Bush's "Jig of Life" come from? Did Kate write it herself, or is it quoted from someone else?
a: Read the credits. The narration is credited to John Carder Bush, and he wrote the text as well as reciting it. Sigh, the liner notes aren't that hard to read.

subject: Another "Where to buy in London?" Question
q: Which bookstores in London carry the Kate Bush biography The Whole Story?
a: Try the Virgin Megastore in Oxford Street. That's the only lead anyone gave, so go look instead of asking the net.

subject: Another GK 250-ML question
q: Can I connect the XLR direct out of my Gallien Kruger 250-ML guitar amp to my stereo aux input to record on cassette, and which wires do I use?
a: Better to buy two line level boxes that bring the external speaker outs down to line level. Then you can use stereo effects and record in stereo. The XLR out is mono anyway, so your wiring plan gets you nothing special.

subject: Guitar like a sitar sound
q: How can I get a sitar-like guitar sound, like in Steely Dan's "Do It Again" and lots of 70's songs? I have a flanger and think one was used.
a: It's not a flanger, kid. Those records used a Coral Electric Sitar, a six-string tuned like a regular guitar, with a flattened bridge for the droning buzz and a set of resonating strings. Coral was tied to Danelectro. They're collector's items now.

subject: Hammond A100 - Question
q: How do I get adjustable distortion out of an old Hammond A100 like the sound Jon Lord got with Deep Purple? And is there a synthesizer with an acceptable organ sound so I don't have to haul the A100 to small gigs?
a: Lord ran his organ through a Marshall guitar amp and then a Leslie cabinet, as on Made in Japan. For a lighter rig, a B-3 sample from a sampler through a guitar overdrive pedal gets surprisingly close, though level-setting takes fiddling. Welcome to tone chasing.

subject: Stereo FX and where to put them
q: How do I hook up a stereo effects unit to two mono guitar amps? Do I use the amps' effects loops, or the guitar inputs on each amp?
a: Doesn't matter. Just plug the stereo outputs into the guitar inputs of the two amps. The in-to-out part of the second amp's loop simply isn't used. Not exactly rocket science.

subject: Bassists! I want to start.
q: I play piano and want to start on bass. What would be a good first bass, and how long should I play fretted before going fretless?
a: Might as well start fretless if that's where you're headed. Fretted gets you going quicker but breeds sloppy habits you'll have to unlearn. As for brands, almost anything will do; try them and pick one you like. Music Man and Rickenbacker are the usual suspects. Don't overthink it.

subject: Mark Knoffler, where are you?
q: It's been years since Brothers in Arms. Does anybody know what Mark Knopfler and Dire Straits are up to these days?
a: Knopfler and three other British musicians formed The Notting Hillbillies and did an album of country classics and some new songs, called Missing... Presumed Having a Good Time. Dire Straits should be touring soon. Keep up, will you?

subject: ES-5 and Boogie - clean sound ?
q: Should an old Gibson ES-5 with three P-90 pickups have all its pickups in phase? Mine's middle pickup was out of phase after repair.
a: Yes, it's supposed to be that way. The bridge pickup is meant to be out of phase with the other two. So the repair shop probably did nothing wrong, and your clean sound problem lies elsewhere.

subject: Advice on distortion pedals
q: What distortion stomp box should my guitarist friend get? Any opinions on the Rat pedal?
a: Distortion is personal taste and the range of sounds is broad. He should take his own guitar and amp, at proper volume, to many stores or borrow pedals from friends. Opinions on the Rat run poor, and DOD and Ibanez Heavy Metal units were liked. Some amps distort fine alone.

subject: Legend amps, what do you know?
q: What do you know about Legend amps? I just bought a Legend Super Lead 50 with a tube preamp and solid state power amp, and I've never heard of the company.
a: Legend came out in the late seventies and lasted five or six years. They were Boogie look-alikes, though the solid state power amp meant not sound-alikes. Ahead of their time, I suppose. Yours probably sold new for $700 to $800, so quit fretting.

subject: Crossroads/Slide/Robert Johnson
q: What tuning did Robert Johnson use for slide, in Crossroads in particular? Any good books, other slide tunings for blues, or tips on slides and practice?
a: Johnson used open E and open G. Arlen Roth's book _Slide Guitar_ has transcriptions of several of his songs. Metal slides sound harsh and nice, bottlenecks sustain well on low strings, and store-bought glass ones are usually worthless. Figure out Crossroads by ear, it's not hard.

subject: The Mellotron
q: Where can I find information on the Mellotron? Was Strawberry Fields the first pop song to use it, and was it really invented by Chamberlin and ripped off?
a: You have the story mostly right. Mellotron settled with Chamberlin out of court, and his version was far superior. Strawberry Fields may well be the first commercial use, per the book Rock Hardware, though the Moody Blues got the big exposure.

subject: Trans Trem - the deal????
q: Why aren't there licensed copies of the Steinberger Trans Trem like the Floyd? Don't patents run out after a while?
a: Patents run 17 years and the TransTrem is far newer, an entirely new system with transposing and locking, so it'll be a LONG time. Licensed Steinberger bass bridges exist, see Hohner. Learn how patents work.

subject: Enya
q: Did Enya make any other CDs besides Watermark?
a: Yes, her solo debut, titled simply Enya. It's mostly the music from the soundtrack of the TV show The Celts, and it's similar to Watermark. Any record store or CD club should have it. Do a little looking yourself.

subject: Midnight Oil
q: Has Midnight Oil's album Blue Sky Mining been released in the States yet?
a: Yes, it came out here a few months ago. Try keeping up with the import bins.

subject: Ever Heard of _Dog Police_?
q: Has anyone heard of a band called Dog Police, with a single of the same name, from a late-night music video show about six or seven years ago?
a: Yes, they were real. If I remember rightly, they won one of the MTV Basement Tapes competitions, and Frank Zappa had something to do with the song. Never heard a peep from them afterward. You didn't dream it, though that's about all I've got.

subject: Has Motown been sold?
q: I heard a rumor that Polygram bought Motown, as they did A&M and Island. Has anyone heard a confirmation or denial?
a: No, Motown has not been sold. They've entered into a distribution agreement with Polygram, which is a different thing. Rumors, honestly.

subject: Goldmine vs. Discoveries
q: I'm thinking of subscribing to either Goldmine or Discoveries. What are the pros and cons of each in article and ad quality, and cost versus content?
a: Goldmine is the better one. Its articles and discographies are first rate, the grading system is clearer and more precise, and the ads are good for promo-only releases. Discoveries just didn't rate with it. Ignore the ads you don't care about.

subject: Lyrics for "extra" verse in "The Boxer".
q: What are the lyrics of the extra verse in Paul Simon's "The Boxer" about "after changes, we are more or less the same"?
a: It's from the Concert in Central Park. The verse goes: Now the years are rolling by me, they are rocking evenly, I am older than I once was, younger than I'll be, but that's not unusual, no it isn't strange, after changes upon changes we are more or less the same. Read the liner notes.

subject: LEVEL 42
q: What ever happened to that new Level 42 disk I heard about here a while back? Last I heard it was released in the U.K. Is it out yet?
a: It's out. Canada has it for about $24CDN, and it's showing up in the states as an import for around $20US. No word on a U.S. release date. Do try to keep up with the news, sigh.

subject: YA "Who Did This Song" question . . .
q: Who did the original version of "Green Tambourine"?
a: The Lemon Pipers, who took it to number one in the winter of 1967-68. No other cover hit the Top 100 in the Billboard book. This comes up every week, you know.

subject: strange vibrations on a screen
q: Why did a friend's Mac screen seem to vibrate when I blew a trumpet loudly in its direction?
a: Probably it was you vibrating. Clench a fork or spoon in your teeth and tweak the end while watching any raster screen and you get the same weird wobble. Your eyes can't follow the small movements against the raster pattern. Hardly rocket science.

subject: K1 ii info sought..
q: Can someone give me the specs of the Kawai K1 II: keys, polyphony, touch sensitivity, connections?
a: It's still made, by the way. 61 keys with velocity and aftertouch, 16-note polyphony, 64 singles plus 32 multis, 256 waves, 32 PCM drum sounds, 16 reverb and delay effects, MIDI in/out/thru. Your shop clerk should have known that.

subject: PX1000
q: Guitar Center is selling the Kurzweil PX1000 piano module for $699. Is it a deal, or would something like the Proteus be better?
a: What killed it for me was the stereo pair as the only outputs, so you can't reverb the strings without reverbing the drums. The Proteus sounded cooler to my ears. There are sibling boxes at $499, and the horn box has the best saxes I've heard.

subject: programming the U-20
q: How programmable is the Roland U-20? Can I access the actual wave tables, or only modify existing patches?
a: It's a sample playback unit, not a synthesizer, so editing is limited. You can change attack, decay, sustain, vibrato and effects, but not the timbre. For truly new sounds you buy extra SN-U110 cards, about $80 each. Learn what you bought before asking.

subject: Cakewalk Pro to Roland MC-50 (Question)
q: I sequence tracks in Cakewalk Pro and need to get them onto a Roland MC-50 while keeping them on separate tracks. Is there any way to dump all the tracks at once?
a: Roland has a new software disk that converts MC sequences to standard MIDI file format, so you could try that, but it costs extra. The free way is to play the sequence over the MIDI line, slave the MC-50 to the clock, record, and extract channels into tracks. Slow, but free.

subject: HR-16 Sysex Info Wanted
q: I want to write my own editor program for the Alesis HR-16 and need its system exclusive information, preferably free. Where can I get it?
a: Ask Alesis. An Alesis rep said it's available for the asking, so go bother them first. If that fails, try the IMA. Honestly, it's not hard to pick up a phone before posting to the whole net.

subject: Yamaha TG33 Question
q: Is it possible to do a keyboard split on the Yamaha TG33 tone generator, perhaps in MULTI mode with some tricky patch programming?
a: Sort of, you don't get much control. Set the level scale of one element to 15 and the other to 16 and you get a split. The EE type must be USER, and you may need to fiddle with the freq shift too.

subject: Problems with SQ-80 and D-110
q: My Roland D-110 freezes and its memory gets scrambled after playing drum tracks sequenced from an Ensoniq SQ-80. What could cause this?
a: There's a known problem where poly-pressure sent to the D-110 can crash it. Set the SQ-80 PRESS setting to OFF when sequencing the drums, and run EDIT, REMOVE CTRLS on the existing track to strip pressure messages. Read your newsletters.

subject: What is a good (cheap) mixer for use with midi rackmount synths?
q: What are some good cheap mixers, in the $100-$300 range, for use with MIDI rackmount synths? I need line level inputs and at least 5 stereo channels.
a: Try a little Peavey mixer: 8 in, 2 out, two effects channels with send/return, panning, headphone jack, two rack spaces, around $170. It's really clean, with no crosstalk feeding a Proteus 1 and a D50 loud. Can't give you the model number, though.

subject: Roland LAPC-1
q: What's a good price for the Roland LAPC-1 card and the MCB-1 MIDI connector box?
a: Anywhere from $350 to $400 for the LAPC is fine, and about $80 for the MCB-1. More MIDI shops are stocking them, and Sierra has always sold the Roland cheap. Shop around, don't pay list.

subject: video styles - (claymation)
q: Was Peter Gabriel the first to use claymation in a music video? Have other artists done it since?
a: No, he wasn't the first. The Go-Go's had a partly claymation video, Get Up And Go, years before. Not as creative, but it's clay animation all the same. Do your homework before crowning firsts.

subject: Training Seeing-Eye Dogs
q: Can I raise a puppy to be a seeing-eye dog while working full time? I'm starved for info.
a: No. Seeing eye dogs are trained by the foundations and assigned to blind people, so you won't get one, and it wouldn't have guide dog privileges anyway. Even raising one for them wants someone home a lot, and you work full time. If you just want a dog, get one from the pound. Your post was confusing.

subject: Do cats get along with ferrets?
q: Do cats get along with ferrets?
a: Usually, yes. Many people keep them together successfully, since cats seem to know ferrets aren't rodents and don't treat them as prey. In most cases the ferret ends up the dominant one. Tips on introductions would depend on your setup.

subject: electronic fencing
q: Has anyone used an electronic fence, where the dog wears a collar that shocks it near the boundary? What does it cost?
a: Invisible Fence buries a wire around your property that triggers the collar. Expect about a thousand dollars, and cheaper if you install it yourself. Catch: a dog chasing another dog may run through the shock and then can't get back in.

subject: Mid-America Cat Fanciers Shows?
q: How can I find out when cat shows are coming up in my area, say Kansas City or Topeka?
a: Look in the back of Cats Magazine or Cat Fancy Magazine. Each lists shows for the next few months in every association, with a number to call for information. Check before driving out, since shows can move unexpectedly. Not hard.

subject: alley cat or purebreed
q: I have two black cats and want to know if they're purebred or mixed. The former owner claimed Angora. Is there a way to tell?
a: Get a book on cat breeds and see which your cats resemble most. But without knowing their lineage, you can't actually know if they're purebred. Sigh, looks alone prove nothing, white neck hairs or not.

subject: Kitten Advice
q: My 8 week old kitten is getting rough, biting and scratching in play, and goes crazy when I eat. Is the roughness a phase, and is it ethical to neuter him in a few months?
a: Neutering is morally mandatory, indoors or out. Otherwise you get howling, or fights and getting lost or hit by a car. He'll grow out of the roughness somewhat, and training it out is your call. Really, you needed to ask?

subject: ANOTHER QUESTION ABOUT SNAKES
q: My baby corn snake keeps staying on the cool side of its tank in the 70s instead of the heated 90 degree side. Any ideas?
a: Corn snakes come from the southern US and northern Mexico, and the 70s end suits them fine. 90 is probably hotter than it wants. Mine do well at room temperature, 65 to 70. Stop fussing and let it pick.

subject: CATS ON TRANQS?
q: My cat keeps marking in the house after a urinary tract infection, and the vet suggests a daily low dose of librium. Has anyone heard of this tranquilizer treatment?
a: Yes, it's not new. Valium has been used for urination problems in cats for over three years, so your vet's 'latest treatment' is hardly cutting edge.

subject: cat using plants as litter box
q: My cat uses my houseplants as a litter box and her digging is killing the plants. How do I stop it?
a: Cut round pieces of window screening, slit them to fit around the plant, and lay them over the dirt. Weigh them down with a brick if she pulls a corner up. Also rule out cystitis or stress, make sure she's spayed, and dump the litter box more often. Cats are not mysterious.

subject: HELP! Rabbit has gone neurotic
q: My rabbit acted fine the day I got back from a five-day holiday, then turned neurotic: hiding, thumping, terrified. What's going on and what should I do?
a: He's probably cross at you for leaving. Rabbits are social and love routine, and being left, even with a sitter, upsets them. Keep your normal routine, spend extra time with him, and be patient. He should eventually forgive you.

subject: Catnip = Dopehead ??
q: What is the chemical in catnip that affects cats so much, and is it addictive or harmful to a cat in the long term?
a: Catnip affects cats much like marijuana affects humans, or so a medical technologist says. As for addiction, cats with fresh catnip in the garden weren't hooked, and one that couldn't get enough dry catnip showed no ill effects when deprived. Nobody gave the chemistry, so look it up.

subject: Question about unusual female dog behavior
q: Why would a fixed female dog hump another, smaller female dog? I've never seen that before. Any explanations besides dominance?
a: It's a dominance maneuver, plain and simple. The larger, older female is showing the younger one who's boss, and males do the same to each other. Hardly a mystery, people.

subject: Picking a Lab puppy
q: How do I pick a good house-dog Lab puppy from a litter of nine at five weeks old? Are there tests or behaviors to watch for?
a: Watching them won't tell you; you'll catch the quiet one in a rowdy mood. Use a published puppy temperament test, scoring each pup 1-5, and run it twice. Ask the breeder too. One such test is in the book Are You my Dog? Do your homework.

subject: RC papers and time in water
q: Can I leave RC papers sitting in a holding tank of water for an hour or two before washing, or hold them some other way?
a: No way. Water and chemicals seep into the paper base at the cut edges, and the fixer is next to impossible to get out. Edges swell and look puffy. Keep total wet time under 10 minutes and wash them one by one.

subject: Can Poor Processing Cause Distorted Prints?
q: Can poor processing at a drugstore photo lab cause distorted negatives or prints, with distortion along the vertical edges?
a: Processing can't distort the negatives, short of melting them. Look at them. If the distortion is on the negative, it's the camera lens, and a really wide-angle one distorts a bit anyway. If the negative is fine, the printer's lens is to blame.

subject: Canon FD -> EOS mount adaptor
q: Does the adaptor for mounting Canon FD lenses on an EOS body work, and who makes it?
a: Canon and third parties both make one, but you don't want it. No autofocus, no focus confirmation, no open-aperture metering, and they act as weak teleconverters. It's a last-chance gadget for super telephoto owners that Canon would rather not discuss.

subject: Colorpainting B&W pictures !!!
q: Has anyone painted color onto black and white photographs? What equipment do I need, and is special paper required?
a: Plain old water colors worked fine for me. Skip RC plastic-coated paper; it won't take them, so use fiber-base paper. Print the images slightly lighter so the color shows even in the black areas. Not rocket science.

subject: HUGE prints, how to make them?
q: Has anyone tried making wall-size photographic prints? I had half-baked ideas like coating a wall with Liquid Light and exposing with a slide projector, or tiling sheets of paper.
a: Just start with big paper. Kodak sells some in wide rolls, and if that's not wide enough you splice it, which means one or two vertical seams in most cases. Far easier than pasting up a pile of 8x10s. Sigh, the wall-coating ideas are overthinking it.

subject: spider webs
q: How do I photograph spider webs with a 50mm lens, especially when there's no dew, like in summer?
a: Webs are thin, so you need real close shots to get any detail. Carry a spray bottle and add water beads to fake a heavy dew. Night shots with flash at different angles work well, and so does an out-of-focus colored background. Basic stuff.

subject: A new body for my Canon FD lenses
q: I have a Canon AE-1 and several FD lenses. Does Canon or anyone make a body that takes FD lenses with multi-mode auto exposure, a multiple exposure button, and LEDs in the viewfinder?
a: Get a T90 or an A-1; both fit FD lenses and should do what you want. The T90 allows any number of multiple exposures on a frame. Expect to pay more than the AE-1 cost new, probably.

subject: Photographing night sky
q: I shot the Northern Lights on Kodak Gold 100 at 15 seconds, f 5.6, as my meter said, but the negatives came out totally clear. What would a better exposure time have been?
a: Your meter is probably fine, but it gets unreliable at the extremes, and you got hit by reciprocity failure. Adams' book on the negative has a chart suggesting closer to 60 or 70 seconds. Bracket around that in 15 second steps. Basic stuff, really.

subject: light meters - recommendations
q: I want a handheld light meter and have looked at Gossen's Luna-Lux, Luna-Pro, Pro-sbc and Pro-F. How do I choose, and is it better than the built-in metering in newer cameras?
a: It depends on the features you need. The Luna Pro F does ambient and flash, and its null metering is great for Zone System work. A flash meter adds buckos but is extremely useful, and the basic Luna Pro is built like a tank. Quantum is cheaper. A meter is just a tool.

subject: very small, manual camera with interchangable lenses
q: I want a very small manual camera with interchangeable lenses, since the optics on the all-automatic point-and-shoot are terrible. What are good used options, and what does an old Rollei cost?
a: Fixed lens: Olympus XA, Rollei 35, Olympus 35 RC, Pen EE. Rollei 35s run from $100 to $400-plus, and collectors' ones top $2000. Interchangeable: old Leicas, Nikon S, Canon rangefinders. A screw-mount Leica IIIf is smaller than many point-and-shoots. Plastic lenses don't cut it.

subject: Pictures from Planes...
q: I'm going up in a small private plane and want to take pictures in the late afternoon over mountains. What film, lenses, filters or equipment do you recommend?
a: Get a UV filter and a polarizer, since altitude UV fools your meter and the polarizer cuts glare. Shoot through the pilot's openable window with the sun behind you, at 1/125th or faster because prop planes vibrate fiercely. A high-wing plane beats a low-wing. Autofocus cameras need a circular polarizer.

subject: Kodachrome processing
q: If you buy Kodachrome with processing included, do you still have to mail it to Canada? Where can I drop off Kodachrome in the SF Bay Area?
a: Mailers with processing included can be honored by Kodalux, though one lab mounted slides despite the mailer saying not to. Kodalux in Palo Alto is one option, but people here have complained about their quality. Take that as you will.

subject: Mamiya 645
q: Is it worth a couple hundred bucks extra to get an old Mamiya 645 instead of the 1000S?
a: Depends how often you use 1/1000 sec. Two hundred seems a huge difference anyway. One got a 645 for $450 with prism, case and filters, and 1000S models turn up around $475. Shop around, don't just pay up.

subject: Film question: Kodak Ektar vs. Fuji vs. ??
q: My shots on Kodak Ektar 125 look washed out and dull. Is it the film, and should I try Fuji Super AG, Kodak Gold, or a different filter?
a: Ektar is cold and runs thin at rated speed; try overexposing about a stop, or try Ektacolor Gold, which has higher saturation and warmer tones. Kodak Gold 100 and 200 are also fine. An 81A filter warms colours but won't intensify them. Learn exposure.

subject: Some Pentax questions
q: What is the difference between Pentax and Takumar lenses? Pentax seems to sell Takumars with KA mount.
a: No real difference. Takumar was the name of Pentax's regular line of top lenses, going back to at least the Spotmatic. Same idea as Minolta's Rokkor lenses. It's a brand name, not a different quality tier. Marketing names, sigh.

subject: washed-out detail; what=cure ?
q: When I photograph a white object with writing on it, the writing looks washed out, and I can't always set exposure manually. What's the best way to avoid this? Will a filter cure it?
a: No filter needed. If white fills the frame, dial your exposure compensation to +2 stops so the darker writing gets enough exposure without losing the white detail. Then put it back to zero when you go back to normal subjects. Don't forget, like everybody does.

subject: black focus ring on Zoom lens
q: Why does half the focusing circle go black on my new 70-200 zoom on an AE-1, and worse with a UV filter on?
a: That's the split-image rangefinder spot darkening with a slow lens. Your f4.5 zoom is not the fast normal lens you're used to, and the filter cuts light further. Swap in a plain ground-glass screen if it bothers you. Learn your optics.

subject: Trunked Radio Systems
q: How are trunked radio systems different from standard repeaters?
a: A trunked system works more like a cellular network. The repeaters are linked to an exchange with automatic channel selection and direct dialing, so you get private calls or group chats. Unlike cellular, there's no hand-over: leave one repeater's coverage and the QSO ends. Basic stuff.

subject: radio shack 2 meter rigs
q: If Radio Shack asks for proof of a ham license and refuses to sell me a 2 meter radio when I won't show it, would I have a case to sue?
a: Probably not. No law forces a retailer to sell to a particular person, except against discrimination of certain groups. One reply thought local ordinances might require stores to sell to everyone unless a sign says otherwise. Go call a lawyer, not the net.

subject: 2m Antenna
q: Is the Cushcraft AR-2 Ringo a good 2m antenna for under $40, or should I consider others?
a: Around here we call the Ringo the Cushcraft Dummy Load. It's cheap and small, but not in the class of an AEA Isopole, a G7, or Comets and Diamonds. If you buy one anyway, coat all joints with NoAlox, since it corrodes rapidly.

subject: NOS->Real OS (Was: memory problems with nos_0531.exe)
q: Have you considered changing NOS into a real network OS, where each network service is a separate program loaded as needed?
a: Yes, and you end up with something awfully like Berkeley UNIX. It already exists, so why reinvent it? 4.4BSD for the 386 is in beta. NOS should keep doing the radio-specific jobs like IP-to-AX.25 encapsulation and low-end MS-DOS clients.

subject: How to get the Tech ticket (was Re: Packet Options)
q: How do I get my Technician class ham ticket, the one that doesn't require a code test?
a: This comes up every week. Call the ARRL for their Prospective Ham Package, or the W5YI Group, to find VE sessions near you. You only need to pass the Novice and Technician theory tests. Since February 15, 1991 no morse code is needed, whatever the study guides say.

subject: Code conversion question
q: Is it possible to convert a file of 6-bit RTTY to plain text, and how do you do it?
a: If you mean Baudot to ASCII, it's painless: a two to one match with upper case ASCII. Track the letters and figures shift characters to pick the right lookup table, which is in the Handbook. If it's cipher, amateurs can't use that anyway.

subject: FTP site for PMP?
q: Where can I find the source for PMP, the Poor Man's Packet, described in 73 magazine in August 91? Are there any well-known amateur archive sites?
a: Grab it from helios.tn.cornell.edu, 128.84.241.2, in /pub. That's the authors' own machine, and version 1.1 superseded 1.0 last I looked. Other sites carry it, but that one is best. There's also an ftpmail server at decwrl if you're stuck without FTP.

subject: New TGV speed record
q: I heard the TGV broke its own speed record last week. Does anyone have details?
a: The previous record was under a year old, at 480 kmh. The new one is just below 510 kmh. That's all I've got without the details in front of me, so don't expect miracles.

subject: CowCatchers, reprise ...
q: Whatever happened to cow catchers on locomotives? Modern diesels have flat fronts that make no effort to deflect an object. Why not an improved cow catcher?
a: They came from the days of free-roaming livestock and lighter locomotives, meant to throw the dead animal clear so it wouldn't derail the lead truck. Enclosure laws cut the cattle, and cow catchers complicated the coupler design, so they went. Against a 30mph impact they wouldn't help anyway. Stay out from under trains.

subject: High speed Quads going slow?
q: Are ski areas running their high-speed detachable quad chairs slower these days? Squaw Valley lift operators said management runs them at 80% to cut maintenance costs. Has anyone got hard facts?
a: Yes, it happens at several places. Park City has run its Prospector quad at 80 to 85 percent of rated speed since it went in, supposedly to keep the number of bodies on the slopes safe. Lifts also get slowed or stopped in high winds. Take half speed over 20 minute lines.

subject: new or used
q: I've skied a few times in Colorado and am tired of renting skis. Should I buy new or used skis?
a: Buy boots first; good, well-fitted boots matter far more than the skis. If you do buy skis, end of season is the time for deals. Used is only worth it if you can check the condition, since skis wear out after about 30 days. Learn that before wasting money.

subject: Binding recommendation needed
q: My wife is an advanced mogul skier on Tyrolia 390s set stiff, and she can't step into them easily. What bindings are easy to step into?
a: Marker. The M46 or the newer M48 have a much more positive step-in action than Tyrolias. The higher-end ones clunk into place so you know you're in. Look at the Marker MRR racing bindings if she wants high DIN numbers.

subject: What is the recomended ski pole length or what do you like?
q: What is the recommended ski pole length, or what do you like?
a: Flip the pole upside-down, grip the shaft just under the basket, and keep your upper arm straight down at your side. If your forearm is parallel to the ground, that's the proper length. Some like it half an inch to an inch shorter, but too short and you miss plants. Too long pushes you back. Not rocket science.

subject: Old Sports Illustrated Article on Future College All-Stars
q: Does anyone remember an old Sports Illustrated article with pictures of future college stars while still in junior high and high school? I only remember Damon Bailey.
a: It was probably the SI college basketball issue for 86-87. Marcus Liberty, Alonzo Mourning and Bailey were in it. Kenny Anderson was named best 9th grader in the country, too. Memory's a fine thing, use it.

subject: NBA: Danny Ferry
q: I heard Danny Ferry was coming back to the NBA. Is that true, and what team is he on?
a: He's with Cleveland. Wilkens likes him for wanting to win and for his passing and floor leadership, and teammates accept his unselfish play. His shot has been giving him trouble. Try reading the papers.

subject: Pickup rules
q: In pickup ball, I shot, the ball hit only the backboard and missed the rim, and I grabbed it and scored. The other team called it an airball and walking because it didn't hit the rim. Was my basket legal?
a: The basket counts. As long as your shot hits anything, rim, glass or another player, you can catch it and do what you want. The NBA rulebook says a try for a field goal must touch backboard or rim. Learn the rules, pal.

subject: bigsky geographical quiz
q: In the Big Sky conference geographical quiz, which cities are Montana and Montana State in?
a: You got the Montanas backwards. Montana State is in Bozeman and the University of Montana is in Missoula. Honestly, it has been all over this newsgroup lately.

subject: UNVL players
q: Is Gerald Paddio still playing for UNLV?
a: No. He left or graduated at the end of the 88-89 season. He now sits on the end of the bench for the Cleveland Cavaliers. Keep up, will you?

subject: Best Record(NBA)
q: What's the most games an NBA team has won before losing its first game, and what's the best season record?
a: The top opening streaks: Washington won 15 in 1948, Boston 14 in 1957, and Seattle 12 in 1982. The Sonics also started 15-0 in 1983 before fading. Season record wasn't answered. Check an almanac.

subject: NCAA Final Four
q: When and where is the NCAA Final Four this year?
a: At the Hoosier Dome in Indianapolis, on March 30 and April 1. The regionals are at Seattle, Pontiac, East Rutherford and Charlotte. Is a schedule that hard to look up?

subject: Run and Shoot (NFL)
q: How would you defend against the Run and Shoot as an NFL defensive coordinator? Blitzing leaves you open to the big play, and some say load up on DBs, like Pittsburgh did against Houston.
a: Pittsburgh's plan was simple: don't get beat deep, and let the small receivers catch short routes, then pound them into the turf. The Oilers' receivers heard footsteps and dropped 11 passes. Not rocket science.

subject: Hurry-up-Offense and drop-kicks
q: In a hurry-up offense with seconds left, can the offense stop the clock by throwing the ball out of bounds, or by committing a penalty like kicking it out or spiking a snap without a set formation?
a: A sideways or backward throw is a lateral, and the clock stops when it goes out of bounds. But there's a rule from the 80s that if you commit a penalty just to stop the clock, the officials can take 10 seconds off. In those cases the half is over.

subject: Auburn vs. Tennessee
q: Is the Auburn vs. Tennessee game going to be on national TV?
a: It's on ESPN in the evening, somewhere between 6:00 and 7:00 depending on who you believe. Check your listings, it's not hard.

subject: rule question
q: The Jets' quarterback throws to a receiver at the 25, who runs to the Dolphins 25 and laterals to another receiver who runs it into the end zone. How long a pass does the quarterback get credit for, and what is the second receiver credited with?
a: The passer gets credit for a 75 yard touchdown pass. The receiver who took the lateral gets credit for the final 25 yards. Basic stuff, really.

subject: McMahon on IR???
q: Does anyone have the status on McMahon, and has he officially been put on the IR list?
a: He will not be put on IR. He's expected out three to four weeks, probably four, after knee surgery on Wednesday. Replays show he wasn't even hit on that play. Try reading the news before begging the masses.

subject: Where's Lafontaine?
q: Pat LaFontaine wasn't suited up in the Canada-USA game. Is he hurt, or just not playing?
a: He has a hip flexor injury, but he's expected to play later in the tourney. Hardly a mystery.

subject: Penalty Shot Question
q: When a player is taken down on a breakaway and awarded a penalty shot, isn't it the team that is awarded it, so anyone can take it? Did the announcer slip up?
a: The announcer was right. The fouled player must take the shot unless injured. A team gets the shot, with any player able to take it, only when no particular player was fouled, like a defenseman covering the puck in the crease. Learn the rulebook.

subject: Team Handball?
q: What is Team Handball like in Europe, and is it played anywhere in the U.S.?
a: It's an Olympic sport and quite popular in northern and eastern Europe, with semiprofessional leagues in Germany and Spain. Sweden, the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia are the best teams. It's played in the US too; it was in the '84 Olympics. Do some reading, kid.

subject: time zones
q: A flight leaves St. Louis at 7:15 pm on August 10th and arrives in Okinawa at 11:10 am on the 12th, crossing the International Date Line. How many hours is the flight?
a: Convert both to UT, it's not rocket science. Departure is 0015 UT Aug 11, arrival 0210 UT Aug 12, so about 25 hours 55 minutes. Assuming Okinawa is UT+9 with no daylight saving. Your watch goes forward a net 14 hours.

subject: KLM and/or Air France
q: Does anyone know KLM's or Air France's phone number here in the USA?
a: Call 1-800-555-1212, toll-free directory assistance, and ask for Air France or KLM. They'll hand it over in seconds. Sigh, you didn't need the whole net for that.

subject: Airline performance records by flight number
q: How can I get airline on-time performance and seat occupancy statistics by flight number?
a: On-time performance is in any airline reservations system for domestic flights, and any travel agent can quote it, rounded down to the next 10%. Seat occupancy is guarded closely for competitive reasons and you won't get it. Dream on.

subject: International Driver's Linense
q: How can I obtain an International Driver's License, and what are the pros and cons of doing so?
a: Go to your local AAA or auto club with your regular license, a passport photo and about $10. It's valid a year and is not a license by itself. It's widely recognized, in a dozen languages. Con: some South American countries want a different kind, so ask.

subject: Getting Married in the UK
q: How easy is it for two US citizens to get married in the UK? What is required for a licence, and are civil services available?
a: Can't speak for the UK itself. France, Portugal and Greece had long waiting periods and banns posted in newspapers. Gibraltar, a British colony, took only 48 to 72 hours with passports, birth certificates and the original divorce decree if divorced. Sleazy, but quick.

subject: Train times in Norway
q: How long do the train trips Amsterdam to Oslo, Oslo to Bergen and Bergen to Bodo take on a Eurail pass, and what is the weather like in Bodo in early July?
a: Amsterdam to Oslo is 15 to 20 hours depending on waits at Hamburg and Copenhagen. Oslo to Bergen is 6 to 7 hours. Bergen to Bodo is about 19 hours. Bodo in July runs anywhere from 10C to 30C. Pack sensibly, it's not hard.

subject: Antarctica
q: I'm interested in commercial and non-commercial (academic, research vessel, etc.) travel to Antarctica. Anyone know where to start looking?
a: Try an up-market cruise such as Society Expeditions, or adventure travel outfits like Mountain Travel or Ecosummer for climbing, trekking and kayaking. Supply ships of the Chilean or Argentinean variety used to take passengers, but nobody knows the current story. Do some legwork, sigh.

subject: Trekking in Nepal
q: I'm planning a group trek in Nepal next April. Is there a difference between full-service tent trips and cheaper 'tea shop' trips, and should I go to Everest or Annapurna?
a: Pros can't run teashop treks, since Nepali law makes them burn kerosene, so teashop is strictly do-it-yourself. Organized runs about $100 a day, DIY under $10. Annapurna is a loop, Everest in-and-out. Read the trekking books, they cover this at length.

subject: Need info. on Hawaiian Airlines
q: I'm planning a trip to Oahu and want to visit other islands. Is Hawaiian Airlines safe, or should I worry about flying between islands?
a: Hawaiian rated worst for satisfaction in Consumer Reports, even below Eastern, which takes talent. Try Aloha Airlines instead, since United books inter-island flights on them. Inter-island flights are as good or bad as any commuter flights, so quit fretting.

subject: Magnetic Island, Queensland
q: Is Magnetic Island in Queensland a good spot for beaches and hiking in early September, or is there somewhere better?
a: Magnetic Island is a short ferry from Townsville and fairly small, but plenty of families and day-trippers show up. Hardly isolated. For real hiking try the Border Ranges on the NSW/Qld border, or Cape York if you want wilderness, crocodiles included.

subject: Thailand
q: Is it safe to go to Thailand in July? A coup took place a few weeks ago; should I cancel my plans?
a: The coup was bloodless, and the Australian government, always over-cautious, hasn't issued a warning. It shouldn't affect much but the parliament; people are too busy making money. Don't cancel on a whim.

subject: travel between England and France
q: What's the cheapest way for two students to get from England to France (Paris)? Is the ferry from Dover to Calais still the way to go?
a: Yes, the Dover to Calais boat is still it, unless you swim. Hovercraft and hydrofoils cost more; the slow boat takes under two hours and is far cheaper. Hunt up a student travel bureau in London and check Let's Go.

subject: Analog tracks are better than digital on LD!
q: A salesman told me the new digital LaserDisc players like the Pioneer LD-870 and CLD-1070 sound worse than the older analog players, and that the press is biased toward digital. Is that true?
a: Nonsense. There's no digital-only player; any digital unit plays the analog tracks too if you push the analog button on the remote. The digital tracks use the CD system, so they sound like a CD unless the D/A converter is lousy. Salesmen, sigh.

subject: Difference between "commercial" and "private" video connectors?
q: Can I just build a cable with RCA on one end and BNC on the other to hook a laserdisc player to an A/V system, or do I need a converter?
a: Just buy RCA to BNC adapters at Radio Shack, they're cheap and people use them between pro and consumer gear all the time. The signal's compatible; video is 75 ohms. Honestly, don't go building cables for a dime part.

subject: Do any of the TR81 clones have...
q: Do any of the TR81 clones have a manual zoom control? I know the TR81 doesn't, but I thought the Fuji or others might.
a: Nope. The Yashica, Kyocera and Ricoh versions all lack manual zoom. Nobody knows about the Fuji. The autozoom is quick enough anyway, and real shooters don't zoom much, so quit fussing.

subject: yasvhsq (yet another s vhs question)
q: Does S-VHS only show its extra resolution on an S-connector TV monitor? And can an S-VHS deck record on a normal VHS tape in normal VHS mode, so lowly VHS owners can play the tapes with hifi audio?
a: It isn't more scan lines, it's more resolution on each line, and you can see it on a plain composite monitor. At least on one RCA deck, yes, it records VHS on VHS or S-VHS tapes, hifi and mono. Not every deck does, so check yours.

subject: Standards & Practice for Camcorder Use & Maintenance
q: Does dubbing S-VHS camcorder tapes to plain VHS for playback copies throw away the quality I bought S-VHS for?
a: Pretty much, yes. An original VHS recording from the camcorder beats a dub from S-VHS, and VHS-to-VHS dubbing is hardly worse than S-VHS-to-VHS. Keep camcorder and deck in the same format, whatever management thinks it's saving.

subject: LD's and Wide Screen Pictures
q: Many of the new laserdiscs I rent are wide screen format, so the picture only fills half to two-thirds of my TV screen. If I could go to full screen height, would I lose a lot of picture?
a: Yes, you'd lose plenty. Panavision or Super Panavision films like 2001 lose about 41% of the picture, and even a 1.85:1 release like ET loses about 28%, nearly a third. Letterboxed laserdisc still beats VHS, so quit whining.

subject: Query based on Sony Critiques
q: On an ordinary Sony TV, does anyone leave the "picture" control all the way up? What does it actually do?
a: Picture is just Sony's name for contrast. Nobody sane leaves it maxed; blacks come out looking grey. Turn it down a bit and raise the separate brightness control to compensate. Read the thing before wasting remote buttons on it.

subject: Laser rot...
q: Several of my laserdiscs show colored dropout dots in the video but not the audio. Is this laser rot, and can anything be done?
a: Yes, that sounds like laser rot. Some of the oldest disks do it. Supposedly disks pressed in recent years have overcome the problem, but time will tell. Not that the manufacturers will tell you.

subject: Classical Video
q: Where can I find reviews of laser discs of performance material like opera and ballet? The Stevenson Guide has very few entries.
a: Try The Laser Disc Gazette, a monthly newsletter that gives about equal space to discs where the audio matters rather than just movies. It's $27.50 for 12 issues, and you can write for a free sample copy. Not exactly hard to find.

subject: Release dates wanted
q: Why are Tremors and Arachnophobia taking so long to reach regular pay cable like Showtime and Cinemax, when they hit Pay-Per-View quickly?
a: If it's a Universal flick, they hold out for more money than Showtime or HBO will pay. CNN said Universal hadn't sold either one a film in eight months. Pay-per-view just tracks the video release date. Greed, as usual.

subject: Dolby Surround Sound and Dolby Pro Logic
q: With Dolby Surround, are there really two distinct rear channels, even though decoders have two rear speakers?
a: No. For home video and 35mm film the two rear speakers get identical signals. Only a 70mm release can have split surrounds, and that's rare. Put them on the side walls, above and just behind you, so the imaging is deliberately bad. Sigh.

subject: best Casblanca LD?
q: What is the best laserdisc version of Casablanca currently available?
a: Depends what you want. The Criterion CAV edition has an outstanding print, an excellent transfer and worthwhile supplements, but costs about $100. The Criterion CLV is similar in quality. A definitive transfer is supposedly coming for the 50th anniversary, so wait if you're picky.

subject: anik e2
q: I've tried to tune in the new Anik Ku bird from Boulder, Colorado, on the 40th parallel, and I see no signal. Should it be visible from here?
a: Probably not. Boulder is likely too far south for the Anik E2 Ku band footprint. One fellow way out in California got about seven channels, half of them scrambled, on the narrowest bandwidth setting, and the picture was barely watchable. Check the footprint before you go hunting.

subject: Renting Wavesailing Equipment in Santa Cruz, CA
q: Does anyone rent wavesailing equipment in Santa Cruz, CA? I'd even pick it up on the Peninsula as long as it's decent gear for ocean sailing.
a: Nobody rents in Santa Cruz that I know of. Up the Peninsula, California Sailboard in San Mateo rents good slalom gear. With the waves lately, slalom or chop hop stuff suits you better anyway.

subject: Fully-cambered sails
q: My buddy's fully-cambered Mistral World Cup sail keeps turning into the wind on a reach and is a struggle to hold. Is that a characteristic of fully-cambered sails or a rigging problem?
a: It's not the camber. Vertical wrinkles mean more outhaul, horizontal wrinkles mean more downhaul. Check your harness line placement, since lines too far back cause this. It may just be an old '86 or '87 race sail, blown out, that slams you. Those didn't hold up.

subject: Help! Mast full of water.
q: My one piece fiberglass windsurfer mast fills with water when the rig goes under, since the original cap and foam plugs are gone. How can I keep it full of air and add some flotation?
a: Two fixes. Hardware stores sell foam in a can, a spray with a tube that expands to fill the cavity, and the mast stops filling. Or put in press-fit foam plugs and seal them with silicone caulking, far enough in that the mast base still fits. Dispose of the can properly.

subject: Evans EV-1 Aircraft
q: I saw an Evans EV-1 aircraft in a museum in Holland, a small single-seat plane with a VW engine, sold as plans by mail. Does the company still exist and who sells the plans?
a: Evans Aircraft is still around, in La Jolla, California. The EV-1 is better known as the Volksplane, a wooden airplane with a VW engine. The VP-1 and VP-2 plans are handled by Aircraft Spruce and Specialty in Fullerton. Do some homework next time.

subject: Meteorite impact in Soviet Union in 1947.
q: A newsletter says a large meteorite hit the Soviet Union in February 1947, near Vladivostok, with the force of an atomic bomb. Does anyone have further information?
a: Scientific American ran an article on it in June 1950, pages 42-43, according to the cumulative index. I've seen photos with trees laid out worse than the Mt. St. Helens blast. Go to a library and look it up.

subject: twins
q: A genetics book said almost all MZ twins are the same sex. How could identical twins ever be different sexes? Was the author just hedging?
a: Probably overcautious, but it can happen. Apparent sex depends on more than chromosomes, like an injured infant surgically changed to female, or a mutation giving an XY female. Excessively rare. Learn some biology.

subject: Birds as descendants of reptiles and knees (Was: Why do we have legs?(Bats?))
q: If birds descend from dinosaurs, why do bird knees seem to face backward, when dinosaurs and everything else have forward-facing knees?
a: Sigh. Birds walk on their toes, and what you call the backward knee is actually the ankle. The real knee faces forward just as ours does. Go look at a cat leg, too.

subject: What is mechanism for bloating of bodies after death?
q: What is the mechanism that causes bodies to bloat after death? Why don't the anaerobic bacteria cause bloating while a person is alive?
a: The immune system is gone, so nothing eliminates the bacteria anymore. The E. coli and other bacteria in the GI tract keep working after death and likely produce carbon dioxide, methane and such. Hence the bloating. Not exactly mysterious.

subject: Modern Pleisiosaur?
q: What was the supposed pleisiosaur hauled out of the water near Christchurch, New Zealand in April 1977? I have a photocopy of a photo of it being lifted by a crane.
a: Sigh, not a plesiosaur. The consensus among knowledgeable people who saw the photo was a badly decomposed, maybe mauled, carcass of a large shark such as a whale shark. Monster hunters never learn.

subject: Looking For Volvox
q: Where is the best place to find Volvox in the wild? Where do they like to be?
a: Try masses of floating plant material, alive or dead, in stagnant water. They seem to need something to attach to and like to be near the surface. And no, not suburban garages, whatever the wise guys say.

subject: Blue LEDs
q: Are blue LEDs available now, who makes them, and how does the cost compare to standard colors?
a: Yes, but wallet-sized pain. Prices run about $12 to $25 each, versus $0.15 for a red one. LEDtronics lists 470 nm parts, and Siemens makes one, but it's dim and easy to ruin with bad bias conditions. Don't expect miracles.

subject: X-10 switches used in 4-way circuit
q: Can I use the X-10 three way switch in a 4-way circuit with three or more switches controlling it?
a: Yes. The non-active half, the Radio Shack Companion Switch, is just a very expensive push button. Wire your existing lines so the companion switches short two parallel lines, and you can use as many as you want.

subject: VCR Replacement Heads
q: Does anyone know a good source for replacement VCR heads? I have an older Sharp with a chipped head.
a: MCM Electronics carries heads for almost any brand of VCR, Sharp included, at roughly $70 to $76 depending on the model. They also sell head alignment tapes and tools. Get their catalog and look it up yourself, it's not rocket science.

subject: big LCS displays?
q: Does anyone know a source for big LCD displays, around 1k by 1k? What do they cost?
a: The real size is 1120x780, an NEC Japanese PC standard. Sanyo sells one as a dual panel with a 16-bit interface, part LCM-5461-24NAK. Hitachi has a 1024x768, LMG9020ZZFC, at roughly 150 to 200 pounds in quantity. Go read the data sheets.

subject: PC layout programs for IBM or Mac
q: Does anyone know of reasonably priced PC board layout programs for the IBM PC or Mac? The ones I've seen for the Mac cost over $1000.
a: For the PC, try Smartwork, PADS and Tango. Look for their ads in Printed Circuit Design magazine. I can't speak for the Mac, so quit expecting a free lunch.

subject: Wire Wrapping Tools
q: Does some company sell wire wrapping tools through a catalog for wire of different gauge than the Radio Shack tool?
a: Sure, look in the Digi-Key catalog. Honestly, flipping through a catalog beats posting to the net.

subject: Battery Storage
q: Does storing unused alkaline batteries in the refrigerator increase their shelf life?
a: Yes. Cold slows the chemical reactions that cause self-discharge on the shelf, roughly halving for each 10 degrees Celsius. Just don't let them freeze, since that can damage them, and let them warm to room temperature before use. Basic chemistry.

subject: Book review ?
q: How can I get my bookstore to order a book if I don't have the publisher and ISBN?
a: Title alone is enough. Any bookseller can look it up in Books in Print and get full ordering information. A place without Books in Print isn't a bookstore. And ISBNs were meant for internal industry use, so stop demanding them.

subject: Bug-Zapper
q: How can I make a homemade electric bug-zapper? Could it be two grid sections hooked to a charged electrolytic capacitor that discharges through the bug?
a: Probably not well. You need a high voltage, around 15KV for a few mm gap, from a TV flyback or a neon transformer, current limited under 20 mA. A lightweight cap can't burn off the corpse. It's lethal, so be careful.

subject: X-10 for remote computer activation
q: How can I power up my computer remotely over the phone and then reach it by modem? Can an X-10 telephone controller do it, given that it needs two calls?
a: Skip the X-10 contraption. Put a DTMF decoder plus a microcontroller between the phone line and the modem and power switch, and have the calling modem send a power-up tone sequence. Or just leave the machine on, which is what I do. Sigh.

subject: Optimod: how does it work ?
q: How does the Optimod from Orban used by radio and TV stations work? Is it just compression and limiting of the dynamic range?
a: Yes, it's just a pretty smart compressor limiter, with six-band compression, wideband limiting and filtering. The idea is to keep the carrier as modulated as possible for as much of the time as possible. Not magic, whatever the marketing says.

subject: need electroluminescent power supply
q: I have an LCD with an electroluminescent backlight panel that needs a few milliamps of AC at 60 to 80 V. Are there small ready-made DC to AC converters for driving these, and where can I get them?
a: Sigh, yes, they exist. Densitron sells six types covering roughly 67-86 volts, and one ran a 2x40 display backlight for about ten bucks from a 5 volt input. Endicott Research Group also makes EL drivers. Call them instead of building a crude doubler chain.

subject: This is really twisted
q: I opened a battery charger for a radio and found two 28-pin DIPs and a crystal inside, an OKI MSM5842 and a National ADC0808. Why would a lousy battery charger need serious logic? What are these chips?
a: Because it's a smart charger, which is the point. The OKI part is a 4 MHz microprocessor with 768 bytes of ROM and 32 nibbles of RAM. The ADC0808 is an 8-bit A/D converter with an 8-channel mux, measuring current or voltage. Somebody finally designed a charger the right way.

subject: Voice recognition help needed
q: I want to build a voice-operated infrared remote so I can say "TV volume up" from the couch. Can it recognize my voice over the TV and room noise?
a: Probably not reliably. Voice recognition is an advanced research topic, not a solved problem. Cheap gadgets manage a tiny vocabulary with lots of errors and no tolerance for noise. Radio Shack sells a chip with about four words, and you don't pick them.

subject: What are good IC references?
q: I'm a beginner in electronics. What are good IC reference books, for TTL and CMOS?
a: National Semiconductor has always had some of the better reference books. Get their LS/S/TTL Databook and the CMOS Logic Databook, not some dusty 1975 edition. Write to them for a literature order.

subject: MODEM SPEED INCREASE - GOT IT
q: If I want to build a 1200+ baud modem for fun, who makes a good inexpensive chip set that doesn't need much glue? I only need it for a dumb terminal.
a: Intel makes a 2-chip set that gives you a complete 2400 baud Hayes compatible modem. You just add the telco interface, a power supply, and RS232 drivers, for around $100 or so. Don't ask me the part number, go read the data sheets.

subject: Weather proofing circuits?
q: Is it OK to coat a PC board with plastic or epoxy to protect it from high humidity?
a: There are chemicals made for exactly this, called conformal coatings. I thought I saw a spray-on kind. Don't go slopping random epoxy on it when the proper stuff exists.

subject: Dimmer switches
q: Is it true that a light on a dimmer switch uses the same amount of electricity no matter the dimmer setting, with a resistor siphoning off the excess?
a: No. Not for a solid-state dimmer, and even with a series resistor the total power goes down when dimmed. Whoever told you that was guessing.

subject: A Challenging PWM Design Problem
q: Is there a simple circuit to turn a PWM signal, 1.0 to 1.9 mS pulses every 18 mS, into a corresponding analog voltage? I can't find a PWM demodulator chip.
a: It's easy: the average DC value rises with pulse width, so all you need is an integrator, a diode, resistor and cap. For precision, use a precision rectifier and an op-amp buffer. Under ten parts. Or abuse an RC servo with a pot, if you like mechanical hacks.

subject: PD CAD software?
q: Is there any public domain or low cost CAD software for schematic drafting or PC board design that runs on a PC under DOS or UNIX, or as an X app?
a: We use OrCAD under DOS and it's moderately priced next to the dozen other packages we demoed. It does schematics, rules check, several netlist formats and SPICE compatibility. No autorouter, though. Not PD, but go read a manual for once.

subject: Rejuvinating Rechargeable Batteries
q: My Sony D7 CD player's rechargeable battery pack has dropped from 4 hours to about an hour after overcharging and running it flat. Is there a way to rejuvenate it?
a: Rechargeable batteries develop a memory. Run them down completely, then charge them for the full time in the instructions. It fixed a portable phone that kept getting shorter run times. Next time, read the manual.

subject: Appropriate use of capacitors
q: What are the appropriate uses, benefits and drawbacks of the various capacitor types: ceramic, tantalum, electrolytic, and film types such as mylar, polystyrene, polypropylene and polycarbonate?
a: Electrolytics give big capacitance at low voltage, but poor accuracy, around +50% -10%. They suit power circuits and general DC filtering. Tantalums are preferable in phono preamps, and polypropylene beats mylar, polyester and polycarbonate for accuracy and bypassing. Read a databook sometime.

subject: Digital circuits from 12v
q: What's required to run 5v TTL and microcontrollers off an automobile's 11-15v power? Do I need a switcher, or is a 7805 okay for a car alarm?
a: Use an automotive-rated regulator like the NatSemi LM2940CT-5.0. It has under 1V dropout and tolerates load dump transients and negative input voltages. Filter the input well, since car power is full of nasty spikes. Use CMOS, run the micro slow, and keep it out from under the hood. A bare 7805 is amateur hour.

subject: Motion Detector (microwave ??)
q: Where can I find a microwave motion detector, or parts to build a burglar alarm based on motion detection?
a: Forget microwave, it's being phased out. Passive infrared units are cheaper and have fewer false alarms. Pull the infrared sensor off a $15 yard light assembly and run it on twelve volts. Surplus microwave alarms turn up from security firms for almost nothing.

subject: Snubbers, free wheeling diodes, and power devices
q: Who are the major manufacturers of thyristors and power devices that I can contact for information?
a: Try Amperex, Powerex, Teccor, AEG Telefunken, GE/RCA Solid State, Gentron, Motorola and International Rectifier. IR and Motorola have good app notes, and IR's catalog could teach a quarter-long course. Use a phone book next time.

subject: Nicads in parallel
q: Why can't nicads be used in parallel to increase current capacity? Larger cells are used for capacity and cells are only linked in series for voltage.
a: Because paralleled voltage sources aren't guaranteed to have precisely the same output voltage, and troublesome things happen. A muscular nicad might try to charge a feeble one, for example. Basic electronics, folks.

subject: naive question about RF propagation
q: Why does AM broadcast radio fade when you drive under a bridge but FM doesn't nearly as much? Does FM propagate better?
a: Think shielded enclosure. Shielding depends on opening size measured in wavelengths. The bridge blocks AM at 0.55 to 1.6 MHz but passes FM at 88 to 108 MHz, where the wavelength is much shorter. Not 'better', just different. Basic physics, people.

subject: IBM Parallel port sillyness
q: Why doesn't a SPDT switch wired to the Acknowledge and PaperOut pins of the parallel port register on compatibles, but works on real IBMs if a printer is plugged in?
a: Compatibles may lack pullup resistors on paper-out, and CMOS inputs have no internal pull-up. They may not even have that signal. Many compatibles aren't truly compatible. Also check you're reading the right LPT address with DEBUG, at 279-27A, 379-37A, 3BD-3BE.

subject: No Batteries in Freezer? (was: Re: AAAA batteries?)
q: Why shouldn't you store batteries in the freezer, as opposed to the fridge?
a: Allegedly, colder freezers will freeze some liquid components of some batteries, while others are likely unaffected. Nobody here actually knows for sure, which is the usual quality of net lore. Hearsay, mostly.

subject: FM audio recording?
q: Why was FM never widely used for audio tape recording? It seems like it would avoid bias circuitry and tape non-linearities.
a: Bandwidth. Audio-quality FM is wideband, roughly 2B plus deviation, so you'd burn so much tape the cost would be exorbitant. FM trades bandwidth for noise performance. Video recorders and Beta Hi-Fi do use it. TANSTAAFL, look it up.

subject: _Numerical Recipes_ Questions
q: Have the routines from Numerical Recipes been put out on diskette for the PC yet? Is there an errata supplement?
a: There's a Pascal version you can grab by ftp as nrpas13.zip, in the turbopas directory under /pc on garbo.uwasa.fi. Nobody here knows about a supplement. Go look yourself.

subject: Any normally-distributed random number functions?
q: I need a C or Fortran function that returns normally distributed pseudorandom numbers with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. What algorithms are there, and is averaging n uniform numbers any good?
a: Averaging uniforms is the terrifying approach. Use CACM Algorithm 488 by Brent, which needs under 1.4 uniform numbers per deviate and is exactly normal. Or transform uniform to normal as in Numerical Recipes in C, page 217. Knuth's Seminumerical Algorithms is the canonical source. Read it.

subject: Inverse of Hilbert matrix
q: How can I find the inverse of an NxN Hilbert matrix as a function of N, rather than just for a given N?
a: Think of the Hilbert matrix as the L^2 inner product on polynomials of degree N-1 over [0,1] in the basis 1, x, x^2 and so on. The Legendre polynomials are the orthonormal basis, so derive the change of basis matrix and square it to get the inverse. Details left to you, as any physicist knows.

subject: unbinding in MACSYMA
q: How do I unbind a variable in MACSYMA? For example, after x:o; how do I put x back to just x?
a: Usually X:'X works as well as anything. To really get X off VARIABLES and INFOLISTS you need KILL(X), which also wipes its properties and assumptions like ASSUME(X>0). Or use BLOCK([X], ...) for local use. Read the manual, it's all there.

subject: Navy Accidents...
q: An aircraft carrier lost sailors and missiles off an elevator in bad weather. Is it routine to run the elevators in such seas, and how big was the wave?
a: Swells were only 4-6 feet, which counts as moderate seas and shouldn't disrupt carrier ops at all. Apparently it was a freak wave nobody expected. Not a routine screwup, so quit gawking.

subject: Unified Germany to use MiG-29s?
q: Is it true that a unified Germany will keep and fly the East German MiG-29s? Has anyone heard anything more on this?
a: Unconfirmed rumor, and I wouldn't trust the source much. West German pilots reportedly hate the cockpit, since the Russians haven't discovered ergonomics yet. The talk is of buying the planes and refitting them with western electronics and cockpits.

subject: Dogtags
q: What information is on a U.S. Army dogtag, the WWII metal disk kind?
a: Last name, then first name and middle initial, service number, blood type, service branch, gas mask size and religion. Pretty basic stuff, and any vet could've told you that.

subject: A-10 Thunderbolt
q: What is the 30mm cannon on the A-10 actually for, if it can't penetrate the front armor of modern tanks?
a: It acts as a sledgehammer, not an armor-piercer. The rounds fall like rain on every exposed part of the tank, including the thin deck armor, and the idea is to shake the tank apart. Look at the demo films before opining.

subject: B52 Replacement (WAS Re: B2 vs. F117A )
q: What's so dumb about designing a heavy bomber variant of a Boeing 747 or some other mass-produced airliner to replace the B52?
a: Nothing, it's not a bad idea. 747s and DC-10s were considered as cruise missile carriers in the late 70s, since a wide-body packs a lot of missiles and saves airframe maintenance. The Air Force just insists on overflying the target. Sigh.

subject: What is the History of Metal Hats?
q: When did soldiers start wearing metal helmets, and what metal was used originally?
a: Around 3000 B.C., give or take a thousand years, to protect the head from maces and axes. They were most likely adaptations of reed, wood or leather helmets, and made of bronze, like nearly everything then. Helmets came centuries before body armor, since heads are fragile.

subject: Computerized Counter Battery Artillery
q: Why do we only hear about aircraft shutting up Iraqi artillery and not our own counter-battery systems?
a: Probably because the Iraqi artillery outranges ours by about 10 km. Kinda hard to counter-battery something you can't reach. That figure came from media sources, so grumble at them if it's off.

subject: Definition of Free Will
q: What IS free will? What does it mean to say people have free will, or that I have free will?
a: Pick a definition. One working version: not all your choices were predictable in principle from the physical state of the universe before life began, nor uncaused and random. Another: the capacity to make choices consistent with your knowledge and values. Philosophers will argue forever, sigh.

subject: theory vs. theorem
q: What's the difference between a scientific theory and a mathematical theorem? Both share a root.
a: At the risk of oversimplification, a theory is a collection of axioms or assumptions. A theorem is a logical consequence of a set of axioms. Not the same animal, and the shared root is no mystery.

subject: Empathy and Sympathy
q: Does feeling empathy require first-hand experience of the situation, or is that sympathy? Can a man empathize with a woman in labor?
a: No first-hand experience needed. Empathy is sharing or experiencing another's feelings, briefly; sympathy adds condolence, agreement or pity. So sympathy needs some empathy plus extras. Any dictionary would settle your dispute, but nobody reads those.

subject: what is science?
q: How do you define science? If by empiricism, then evolution has been validated. If not, what is your definition?
a: The Oxford dictionary calls it truths based on observation, experiment and induction. So how much evolution have we actually observed? Sigh, look it up before arguing.

subject: "new" Space Life Science
q: Are NASA's "new" space life science findings really new? Haven't the Soviets already found these things, and how much cross-program learning goes on?
a: I doubt the Soviets did anything like it. Their data is bulk quantities, such as blood pressure, pulse and temperature, taken a few times a day, plus detailed data after landing. These experiments took continuous measurements through launch and the first days in orbit. Read the actual papers.

subject: Galileo encounters with Venus and Terra
q: Did we get any telemetry from the Galileo Venus encounter, either scientific data or images? Are there plans to do the same with the two Terran flybys?
a: Yes to both. And in English the planet is called Earth, not Terra. Honestly.

subject: Pharmacies in Space
q: Does anyone know good articles about pharmaceutical labs or genetic engineering in earth orbit using zero g?
a: Mostly NASA-encouraged propaganda to sell the space station. McDonnell-Douglas's electrophoresis project got obsoleted by earth-based separation and was terminated. Genetic engineering needs no microgravity. The one real use is growing large protein crystals for structure determination.

subject: Galileo image compression?
q: Does the Galileo spacecraft have any capability to compress images on board before transmitting them, and will that be used for Jupiter pictures?
a: If memory serves, Galileo does have limited image compression and uses it for all picture transmission. I'd check my books, but they're packed away. Stop assuming they send raw data like a toy.

subject: COMPARISON OF PROBE TECHNOLOGY
q: How does the technology of Pioneer, Voyager and Viking compare with Magellan, Ulysses, Galileo and the HST? Is it a next generation, or the same basic things for different missions?
a: No sharp generation boundaries, just gradual evolution. Mariner 10 was far beyond Mariner 2, so be more specific. The real gap comes after your list, between Magellan, Ulysses, Galileo and HST (mostly ten-year-old hardware) and Mars Observer.

subject: Oxygen recycling
q: How have long-duration spacecraft and stations handled the crew's oxygen? Do they just carry stored oxygen, or has anyone tried recycling it with a greenhouse of plants or a chemical system?
a: Everybody so far has used stored oxygen and chemical CO2 removal. The US uses liquid oxygen and lithium hydroxide; the Soviets add potassium oxide, which does both jobs. Greenhouses eat too much mass, volume and energy, so they only make sense on a planetary surface. Sigh.

subject: Antimatter Drives.
q: I read Robert Forward's book Mirror Matter, which says practical use of antimatter is now possible. Are his ideas impractical? If not, what is being done about them?
a: They look practical, but nobody's putting big bucks into it. Small projects work on handling antiprotons, and the USAF funds some propulsion study. No fundamental obstacles found, but lots of engineering is needed, and fast results cost money. The only proven use so far is making Nobel Prizes.

subject: Gravity vs. Mass
q: If you dug a hole clean through the earth and fell in, would you weigh a huge amount at the center or be weightless, since you're surrounded by equal mass?
a: Weightless, any fool knows that. Spherically symmetric mass gives zero gravity at the center, and you're in freefall the whole way, oscillating in simple harmonic motion for constant density. Strictly, the Sun and Moon would tug at you a bit.

subject: Is the moon upsidedown to NASA?
q: In Australia the full moon looks like a rabbit with big ears on the left. Is it upside down in the northern hemisphere?
a: Yes. Everyone knows the Moon viewed from the northern hemisphere is the other way up from Australia. Someone who moved north from New Zealand confirms it. Not exactly rocket science, though this is sci.space.

subject: Giotto (was:"Re: Some comments on comments...")
q: Is Giotto still functional after the Halley mission? What is it doing now, and what are its mission plans?
a: It survived Halley with some damage, nobody's sure how well the camera works, and it's hibernating in solar orbit. ESA plans to wake it and test it. If all goes well, an Earth flyby on July 2, 1990 could redirect it to comet Grigg-Skellerup on July 10, 1992.

subject: S-Band Beacon on Moon
q: Is the Apollo transmitter on the Moon still operating? It's supposedly a beacon around 2.3 GHz used by moonbounce amateurs.
a: Doubtful. As far as I know, all the Apollo surface transmitters were shut off when the seismometer network was shut down, to save some trifling amount of money. The only Apollo surface devices still useful are the laser retroreflectors. I could be wrong.

subject: Skylab
q: Was there ever any real chance of saving Skylab with the space shuttle? Would it have been worth it?
a: There was some chance, and a rescue was even planned for the second shuttle flight. But Skylab came down earlier than expected and the shuttle flew later than expected. Worth it? Doubtful. The thing had no provisions for resupply or repair, so don't get misty-eyed.

subject: Private Space Industries -- What's up?
q: What's going on with Amroc since their recent launch failure, and are they going to try again? What about SSI of Houston?
a: Amroc took a setback and laid off people, but they plan to try again. The payloads were almost undamaged, whatever the early reports said. SSI still has no orbital customers, last I heard, just sounding-rocket flights for NASA researchers. Not exactly thrilling.

subject: Recovery of Salyut 7
q: Why are the Soviets planning to recover Salyut 7 using Buran? Is it to test Buran, keep it from crashing, study long-term exposure in LEO, or something else?
a: Mostly to study it. Haul it down in one piece and you can take it apart on the ground and see how materials and machinery wear after long exposure to orbit. That's the usual Soviet method: build short-lived, analyze failures, redesign. Someone also mentioned showing it off at the Paris air show.

subject: Saturn V and Design Reuse: Saturn VI?
q: Why rebuild the Saturn V instead of improving the design into a Saturn VI with 30 years of better technology?
a: There's no technical reason we can't build a better booster, but politics, paper studies and creeping featurism kill every such project. Reviving the Saturn V dodges that. Get something that flies first, then improve it.

subject: Gaspra Data to come soon??? (Re: Galileo Update - 11/05/91)
q: Will we get the Gaspra image from Galileo early, or only after a long wait?
a: One Gaspra image will be sent back early. The project has 70 meter antenna time until November 20, so they can send it at 40 bps. Patience.

subject: More than one shuttle at a time?
q: Has NASA ever looked at or planned a shuttle mission with more than one orbiter in space at the same time?
a: This comes up so often it nearly made the FAQ. Nobody has planned it recently. Before Challenger, dual-ops projects were in the works for a 26 flights a year dream, but reality set in at about 12 to 13 flights. Support facilities would need upgrading anyway.

subject: Are two missions possible (Was Satellite)
q: Is it really that hard for the shuttle to go up with one satellite and come back with another, or otherwise combine missions? I thought the problem was just available space.
a: Space isn't the biggie. Orbit is. You need a payload happy to sit in exactly the same orbit as the bird you want to retrieve, and big orbit changes eat fuel, so it's impractical. Payload-bay fittings add complications too.

subject: alternate launch vehicles
q: Is the British air-breathing shuttle project, HOTOL, completely dead?
a: Not quite dead, but the pulse is dangerously low. AW&ST says the British Government stopped funding it, though British Aerospace is negotiating with private concerns to continue. Typical government response to aerospace, sigh.

subject: Barbara Boxer
q: What are Barbara Boxer's views on space? Is she worth sending campaign funds to?
a: Mixed. The Space Activist's Handbook scores her 20 percent on the votes she cast, and she's in the House Space Caucus. She grilled NASA on station financing. Call her office if you want more. Get off the net and ask.

subject: Space Shuttle Electronics
q: What processors, memory, clock speed and programming language are used in the space shuttle's computers? Is it classified?
a: This is about to make the most-asked-questions list; it's been answered several times already. Nothing about the shuttle is classified. It's all public knowledge, and only certain payloads and missions are secret. Check the archives first.

subject: Space Shuttle fashions
q: Why did the shuttle crews switch from orange pressure suits to blue ones and back to orange again?
a: Nobody really knows why they went from blue to orange. What's known is the new suits are real pressure suits, needed for the new high-altitude escape system on landing. Early flights used orange suits like the SR-71 ones until the shuttle was deemed operational. Fashion, bah.

subject: Shuttle Payload Questions
q: Why does Columbia get left behind, and is there a reason Atlantis is the usual orbiter for DoD missions? Is Columbia being retrofitted to match the rest of the fleet?
a: Columbia is older and heavier, and later orbiters got improvements. There's no preference for Atlantis; Columbia is just excluded from weight-critical missions, which DoD ones tend to be. She's slated as the long-duration Spacelab orbiter, since bringing her up to spec would cost nearly a new orbiter.

subject: Why is voluntary work excluded?
q: Why is voluntary work specifically excluded during a government shutdown? Is it to close the installation completely or something more obscure?
a: Mostly liability and responsibility, plus protecting workers from management demanding non-voluntary voluntary work. Unpaid people aren't employees, so hazard and comp arrangements go void. Also some brinksmanship: inspectors coming in anyway would kill the leverage. Politics, naturally.

subject: Multiple Screens for Stereo Imaging
q: How can I get a Silicon Graphics machine to drive two separate TV screens at once, with a different window on each?
a: If you really mean TV screens, the SGI Video Splitter board may do it. It splits the console into up to four lower-resolution outputs from windows, frame-synchronous, with genlock options. It's pricey, around $15-20K. Don't know of anything else that does it.

subject: Sega glasses
q: I've heard of the Nintendo powerglove, but what are the Sega glasses?
a: They have two LCD shutters, one over each eye, with one open at a time. Sync them with two stereoscopic images on the screen and you get 3D. They're cheap, built for the Sega home system, but the shutters don't fully block when closed. Don't expect miracles.

subject: Stafford Loans and other stuff ....
q: I'm starting grad school and may not get by on my stipend. Is it hard to get Stafford loans as a grad student, and does the process work like it did for undergrad?
